articles.title: Judge's Great Yarmouth exhibition shines light on roller skating
articles.summary: A national roller skating judge and photographer hopes the sport can one day be in the Olympics.
articles.body:
A roller skating enthusiast who has captured the lives of seven artistic skaters over 10 years hopes her exhibition can shine a spotlight on the sport.

Debby Besford grew up in Great Yarmouth, Norfolk, which has a strong roller skating heritage, and travelled all over the country to compete.

While flicking through photo albums on a visit to her parents and reminiscing over her skating days, she decided it would be "fantastic" to do an exhibition about young skaters from the town's Retro Skating Academy.

She said it was "amazing" to see how skating had shaped their lives during the decade.

Besford said roller skating had been "very, very important for many, many years" to Great Yarmouth, with the town producing a number of champions.

She said the Victorian Winter Gardens on the seafront, which used to house a prominent rink and is undergoing restoration , was "a place that was like my creative space and my safe space as well, and to have another family of skaters and parents to support you".

She has been loaned various items of memorabilia which also feature in her exhibition called The Art of Roller Skating, based at the town's Time and Tide Museum until April.

Artistic roller skating is not yet recognised as an Olympic sport, which Besford said she wanted to put under the spotlight in her exhibition.

GB Skate Artistic, Britain's governing body , said not being an Olympic sport meant it struggled to gain funding, adding that it believed every nation was striving to see it one day get accepted.

Skate Norfolk runs sessions for children and adults across the county and said roller skating was much more popular than it was 10 years ago.

"We are busy, we just do not have enough volunteers to run more sessions," said a spokesperson.

Speaking about her photography, Besford said she wanted to remove the skaters from the intensity of the rink and portray them in everyday life in their bedrooms, alongside their array of medals and trophies.

She has seen them all grow from young teenagers into adulthood.

"They're all doing incredibly well, with going to university, having careers," she said.

"Their connection with the sport has very much influenced in the way that they think, and the way they believe in themselves as young adults now."

articles.title: John Nicks Dies at 97, Figure Skating Hall of Famer Coached Peggy Fleming, Ashley Wagner, More
articles.summary: Legendary figure skating coach John Nicks died Tuesday at the age of 97.
articles.body:
Legendary figure skating coach John Nicks died Tuesday at the age of 97.

"The skating community has lost a tremendous ambassador," U.S. Figure Skating chief executive Matt Farrell said, per the Associated Press' Dave Skretta . "John helped shape generations of American figure skaters and his influence extended well beyond the champions he coached."

Nicks was a decorated skater in his own right. Teaming with sister Jennifer, he won gold in the pairs competition at the 1953 World Championships. They were also silver medalists in 1950 and earned bronze in 1951 and 1952.

Serena, Jeter, More in New 'Speed Goes Pro' Trailer 🎬

Woman Dies Running Marathon for Charity (AP)

LeBron's KD and Steph Scouting Reports 📋

Nicks left a larger legacy after pivoting to coaching.

Peggy Fleming, Sasha Cohen, Ashley Wagner and Kristi Yamaguchi are among the decorated skaters he worked with through the years. Skretta noted the overall total eclipsed 1,200 figure skaters.

"Mr Nicks, you were a champion maker," Wagner said in an Instagram post . "I will forever be grateful for my time with you, the lessons learned and the athlete that you transformed me into. You made me understand that I had to skate for the person sitting in the last row, at the top of the arena. You made me a performer, a skater who learned to care so much more about the total package, instead of just the jumps. Thank you for making me a champion, I would not be where I am today if it were not for you."

U.S. Figure Skating inducted Nicks into its Hall of Fame in 1993, and he earned a spot in the World Figure Skating Hall of Fame in 2000.

articles.title: History! 15-year-old Tanvi Patri becomes first Indian woman to reach Youth Olympic badminton final
articles.summary: India's Tanvi Patri scripted history on Wednesday by becoming the first Indian woman to reach the badminton final at the Youth Olympic Games.
articles.body: India's Tanvi Patri scripted history on Wednesday by becoming the first Indian woman to reach the badminton final at the Youth Olympic Games. The 15-year-old defeated Japan's Yuzuno Watanabe 21-14, 11-21, 21-19 in a thrilling three-game semifinal in Buenos Aires. The Odisha shuttler showed great fighting spirit to overcome her opponent and move within one win of a historic gold medal.Tanvi had to work hard for the victory after Watanabe bounced back strongly in the second game. However, the Indian kept her calm in the deciding game and came up with some attacking shots to seal the contest. The victory was also a sweet revenge for Tanvi, who had lost to Watanabe 21-14, 21-10 in their previous meeting in Thailand.Before her, only three Indian shuttlers - HS Prannoy, Lakshya Sen and Aditya Joshi - had reached the badminton semifinals at the competition.Prannoy won silver at the inaugural Youth Olympic Games in Singapore in 2010. Lakshya also finished with a silver medal at the 2018 edition in Buenos Aires. Aditya, meanwhile, reached the boys' singles semifinals in 2014 but returned without a medal.Tanvi has already made a name for herself in junior badminton. She earlier won the girls' singles U-17 title at the Badminton Asia U-17 and U-15 Championships in Chengdu, becoming the first Indian shuttler to win both continental titles.Now, the 15-year-old has a chance to create another piece of history. One more victory will give her a Youth Olympic gold medal and make her achievement even more special.More to follow ...Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Olympic gold, Asiad medals stolen from hockey legend MM Somaya's Bengaluru home
articles.summary: BENGALURU: Last Wednesday, when hockey legend MM Somaya returned from his morning walk in Apangela, near his hometown Madikeri, his wife Shami greeted him
articles.body: BENGALURU: Last Wednesday, when hockey legend MM Somaya returned from his morning walk in Apangela, near his hometown Madikeri, his wife Shami greeted him with news of a burglary at their Bengaluru residence.His first thoughts were about his most prized possessions - medals won for the country, including his gold medal from 1980 Moscow Olympics. He rushed back to find his worst fears confirmed. His house in HAL 3rd Stage had been broken into between 2.30am and 4am on Oct 28, and valuables worth over Rs 3 lakh, including four international medals, were stolen."I'm obviously very hurt because the medals are an irreplaceable symbol of years of dedication, sacrifice and service to the country," an anguished Somaya told TOI.The two burglars, wearing helmets, also stole Rs 30,000 in cash and gold and silver articles. They entered after breaking open the main door and were captured on neighbours' CCTV cameras."Apart from the Olympic gold, two Asian Games medals - a silver from the 1982 Games in New Delhi and a bronze from the 1986 Games in Seoul - and a Champions Trophy bronze from 1982 were stolen," Somaya (67) added.Neighbours alerted the couple around 7.30am, and they immediately left for Bengaluru. Police registered an FIR the same day and said they were confident of solving the case, citing strong clues."We have collected much CCTV footage from the area and have some vital clues on the miscreants. They had watched the house for some hours and, after ensuring it was locked, broke in. However, we will crack the case," an investigating officer said.Somaya, a former India captain, moved to the city from Mumbai in 2025 after retiring from Bharat Petroleum.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bengaluru | Silver Rate in Bengaluru | Bank Holidays in Bengaluru | Public Holidays in Bengaluru | Bengaluru AQI | Weather in Bengaluru | Petrol Price in Bengaluru | Diesel Price in Bengaluru | CNG Price in Bengaluru | LPG Price in BengaluruStay updated with the latest Bengaluru news. articles.title: ‘Everybody can play on turf’: Dutch Olympic champion explains where India are falling behind
articles.summary: Mohali: Former Netherlands hockey star Floris jan Bovelander believes India’s vast talent pool can only translate into sustained global success if the
articles.body: Mohali: Former Netherlands hockey star Floris jan Bovelander believes India’s vast talent pool can only translate into sustained global success if the country improves access to artificial turf pitches and strengthens grassroots development programmes.In Punjab for the Asian Champions Trophy, Bovelander, who has been involved in hockey development projects in India for more than a decade, said the biggest difference between hockey powers such as the Netherlands and India remained infrastructure at the grassroots level.“We have more than a thousand turf pitches in the Netherlands and all kids start on turf pitches,” Bovelander said. “The techniques and tactics of modern hockey are easier to learn when you play on turf from a young age.”While India possesses a far larger playing base, he noted that many pitches remain concentrated in stadiums and elite centres, limiting access for young players.“You have pitches, but sometimes you’re not allowed to play on them because they’re in stadiums. In the Netherlands, everybody can play on the turf pitches. That’s important for development,” said the two-time Olympic gold medallist.Bovelander, who helped establish the Naval Tata Hockey Academy in Jharkhand and remains involved in community-based programmes through the Bovelander Foundation, stressed that infrastructure alone was not enough.“There is often a lot of focus on high performance, but high-performance hockey benefits from strong grassroots programmes,” he added. “You need festivals, school competitions, youth leagues and good coaching. Elite players inspire young children, but you also need a strong base underneath.”As for the Indian men’s team, Bovelander said it had developed into one of the world’s most difficult sides to beat, citing back-to-back Olympic bronze medals as evidence of its progress. However, he admitted India had occasionally fallen short in key moments at major tournaments.“They are one of the top teams in the world. Maybe they are missing a little bit in the key moments, but they are always there,” he said. “If things go their way at one of the next major tournaments, they can win.”Bovelander also called for a healthy balance between experienced players and emerging talent, saying national teams should avoid relying on reputation alone.“Players should be in the team because of their performances, not because of their history,” he said. “Young players must keep pushing the experienced ones.”India’s 2016 Junior World Cup-winning generation had gone on to form the backbone of the senior side, he noted, but the challenge now was ensuring the next crop of youngsters was given similar opportunities.As far as his discussions with Punjab’s administration is concerned, Bovelander said he hoped to explore ways of contributing to coaching and grassroots initiatives, adding that expanding access to playing facilities would be among the issues he would raise with policymakers.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: La Nationale-Nederlanden San Silvestre Vallecana, una carrera de moda
articles.standfirst: La prueba, que continúa batiendo récords en su 62º edición, renueva su acuerdo con MARCA. Laura Luengo, plusmarquista española de medio maratón, es la madrina de este año
articles.summary: La prueba, que continúa batiendo récords en su 62º edición, renueva su acuerdo con MARCA
articles.body: Unos corren disfrazados, otros lo hacen con sus mejores galas. La Nationale-Nederlanden San Silvestre Vallecana, la fiesta del atletismo que se disputa por las calles de Madrid el último día del año desde hace 62 ediciones, sigue de moda un año más. La legendaria carrera, que ayer renovó su acuerdo con MARCA, mantiene su esencia pero continúa innovando y batiendo récords. En 2026, la esperada camiseta, uno de los símbolos de esta prueba, ha sido diseñada por la firma madrileña OTEYZA. “La mentalidad de Nationale-Nederlanden es muy emprendedora”, asegura Juan Perteguer, Subdirector general y Chief Marketing Officer de Nationale-Nederlanden. “Este año hemos convertido la carrera en una pasarela de moda. Además, es una moda sostenible, que está muy alineado también con nuestros valores. Al final si queremos estar cerca de nuestros clientes, tenemos que estar cerca también de las tendencias y de lo que realmente les motiva a ellos”. Un año más, 42.000 corredores disputarán la prueba por las calles de Madrid, 2.000 de ellos en la carrera de élite, en la que volverá a estar Laura Luengo, flamante plusmarquista nacional de medio maratón, tras firmar 1.08:28 en Valencia hace diez días. “La Nationale-Nederlanden San Silvestre Vallecana es un momentazo”, asegura la atleta. “Siempre que me pongo en la línea de salida pienso que tengo que disfrutar para acabar el año haciendo lo que más nos gusta, con un ambiente increíble. Haces también un repaso al año atlético y te ayuda a poner ese punto final dulce al 2026 en una carrera tan especial y emotiva”. La Nationale-Nederlanden San Silvestre Vallecana aglutina la élite y el atletismo popular, corredores que disputan la carrera para hacer marca y los que sólo quieren disfrutar de la fiesta el día 31 de diciembre. “Una de las razones por las que llevamos tantos años patrocinando esta carrera es precisamente que no es una carrera excluyente, puede correrla cualquiera, desde un profesional de alto rendimiento a una familia con niños que quiere pasar una tarde agradable”, asegura Juan Perteguer. “Para nosotros los clientes al final son personas con sus casuísticas, con sus necesidades, independientemente de lo profesional que pueda ser. Una carrera que es para todos es el lugar donde nos sentimos cómodos”. Por último, Antonio Sabugueiro, Secretario general de la Agrupación Deportiva San Silvestre, destacó en MARCA que “al principio pensamos que esto sería una carrerilla, nunca imaginamos que haríamos una prueba como ésta. Somos una familia y yo creo que ése es el uno de los grandes éxitos de la Nationale-Nederlanden San Silvestre Vallecana”.Sin duda, una carrera que sigue de moda.

articles.title: ISSF World Championships: India add another team silver, but Olympic quota wait continues as Manu Bhaker, Suruchi Singh falter in final
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India added another team silver to their medal tally at the ISSF World Championships in Doha on Thursday, but the wait for an individual medal
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India added another team silver to their medal tally at the ISSF World Championships in Doha on Thursday, but the wait for an individual medal and a coveted 2028 Los Angeles Olympics quota continued after Manu Bhaker and Suruchi Inder Singh faltered in the women's 10m air pistol final.The two Indian shooters, who had qualified for the eight-shooter final, finished outside the medal positions. Double Olympic bronze medallist Manu placed fifth with 179.9 points, while Suruchi, an Asian Games mixed team gold medallist, was sixth with 158.3.China's Jiang Ranxin clinched the gold medal with 242.4 points, narrowly edging compatriot Yao Qianxun, who took silver with 242.1. Hungary's Veronika Major completed the podium with 222.1. All three medallists also secured quota places for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, leaving the Indian duo without a ticket to the Games.Manu, Suruchi unable to capitalise on final spotsManu struggled to find consistency in the final, with her scores fluctuating between 8.8 and 10.7. The 24-year-old was eliminated after the 18th shot, ending her hopes of adding a World Championships individual medal to her impressive collection.Suruchi also endured a difficult final, with a series of shots in the 8s and 9s proving costly. She bowed out after the 16th shot, bringing India's challenge in the individual event to an end.Both had shown enough in qualification to raise hopes of a strong finish. Manu recovered from a modest start, shooting 95 in each of her first two series before producing scores of 98, 100, 96 and 99 to finish third with 583 points.Suruchi secured the eighth and final spot with 580. She shot 97, 95, 96, 97, 97 and 98 across her six series to scrape into the final. China's Jiang topped qualification with 585, while India's third entrant, Sainyam, finished 22nd with 575.Team silver offers consolation, but no Olympic quotaThere was some consolation for India as Manu, Suruchi and Sainyam combined to secure the silver medal in the team event with an aggregate of 1,738 points. China won gold with 1,745.The team standings were determined by the combined qualification scores of the three shooters from each country. Sainyam's contribution proved important in India's podium finish, even though she missed out on the individual final.However, the team silver does not carry an Olympic quota. The Doha World Championships are the first major shooting competition offering individual quota places for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, making the missed opportunity particularly significant for India.Despite adding another team medal to their campaign, Indian shooters are yet to win an individual medal or secure a quota place in an Olympic discipline at the championships. Manu and Suruchi's disappointing finishes have therefore extended India's wait for a breakthrough in the individual events.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: India roar back from 0-1 down to beat Japan 4-1, clinch record sixth Asian Champions Trophy title
articles.summary: India scripted history on Thursday, clinching a record sixth men's Asian Champions Trophy title after producing a stunning comeback to defeat Japan 4-1 in
articles.body: India scripted history on Thursday, clinching a record sixth men's Asian Champions Trophy title after producing a stunning comeback to defeat Japan 4-1 in the final in Mohali.The victory also completed a hat-trick of consecutive Asian Champions Trophy titles for India, who continued their dominance in the continental competition. It was a special night for the hosts, who bounced back from a frustrating first half to deliver a commanding performance when it mattered most.Shilanand Lakra (42nd minute), Dilpreet Singh (48th), Jugraj Singh (53rd) and Vivek Sagar Prasad (54th) were on target for India after Japan had taken an early lead through Kazumasa Matsumoto in the third minute.Japan strike early, India struggle to find a breakthroughJapan stunned the home crowd by taking the lead in the third minute. Matsumoto collected the ball on the left, made his way into the circle and unleashed a powerful reverse-hit effort that beat Indian goalkeeper Suraj Karkera.India looked to respond and enjoyed spells of possession, but Japan's disciplined defensive structure made it difficult for the hosts to create clear-cut opportunities. The Indian attack struggled to find its rhythm, while the Japanese defenders stood firm and limited the hosts' scoring chances.India had a few opportunities through Abhishek and Hardik Singh, but their efforts failed to trouble the Japanese goalkeeper enough. The hosts also lost an early review after an appeal for a push inside the circle was turned down.Japan continued to frustrate India in the second quarter, earning penalty corners and testing the Indian defence. Amit Rohidas produced a crucial block to deny Fujishima, while the visitors maintained their organisation at the back.India went into the half-time break trailing 0-1 and still searching for their first penalty corner of the match.Shilanand sparks India's comebackIndia returned with greater intent after the break and gradually began putting Japan under pressure. Harmanpreet Singh, who had been one of the tournament's leading goal-scorers, came close with a penalty-corner effort, but Japanese goalkeeper Kisho Kuroda stood firm.Sukhjeet Singh also saw an attempt saved, before Harmanpreet's reverse-flick from the rebound struck the post. Despite the mounting pressure, Japan continued to hold on to their lead. The breakthrough finally arrived in the 42nd minute. India earned a penalty corner and, after Harmanpreet's attempts were kept out by Kuroda, the hosts continued to attack. Aditya produced a superb reverse-flick pass, which Shilanand Lakra converted from close range to make it 1-1.Japan challenged the goal, claiming that Aditya's pass was dangerous, but the TV umpire found no clear reason to overturn the on-field decision. The goal stood, bringing India back into the contest.India run riot in final quarterWith the scores level heading into the final quarter, India raised their intensity and took control of the contest.Hardik Singh played a key role in India's second goal in the 48th minute. Showing excellent composure under pressure inside the circle, he recovered possession after his initial pass was blocked and set up Dilpreet Singh. The forward took a touch before producing a brilliant finish with his back to the goalkeeper to put India ahead for the first time.The hosts extended their advantage five minutes later. Vivek Sagar Prasad intercepted a pass in midfield before the ball reached Sukhjeet, whose effort earned India a penalty corner. Jugraj Singh stepped up and unleashed a thunderous drag-flick to make it 3-1 in the 53rd minute.India struck again just a minute later to put the result beyond Japan's reach. Nilakanta Sharma won a loose ball and initiated the move, with Shilanand's initial effort saved by the goalkeeper. The rebound fell to Vivek Sagar Prasad, who smashed it past the keeper with a superb half-volley to make it 4-1.Japan earned one final penalty corner with 10 seconds remaining, but India's defence blocked the drag-flick to bring the contest to an end.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Youth Olympic Games: Wushu among new sports catching the eye at Dakar 2026
articles.summary: Chinese martial art wushu taolu has been among the eye-catching events debuting at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games.
articles.body:
After a spectacular opening ceremony which celebrated Senegalese national identity and wider African culture on Saturday, the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympics are in full swing.

The continent's first ever Olympic event is showcasing new sports which have never appeared at any version of the Games before and has offered athletes predominantly aged 15 to 17 a place in the history books.

First-time Olympic medallists have been crowned in baseball5 and wushu taolu, while some of the rowers who secured places on the podium in coastal beach sprint events may well be eyeing up potential glory at the senior Los Angeles 2028 Games.

BBC Sport Africa examines what has attracted the most attention during the first week of competition.

Arguably the most eye-catching sport on show in Senegal has been this modern Chinese martial art, better known around the world as kung fu and practiced competitively in two forms via choreographed sequences or sparring.

Promoted by the government of the People's Republic of China to encourage friendly international exchange, the International Wushu Federation was established in 1990 to formalise centuries-old disciplines popularised by the likes of movie stars Bruce Lee, Jackie Chan and Michelle Yeoh.

Wushu has featured as an exhibition event or part of the cultural programme at past Games, but medals in changquan and tajiquan were up for grabs on its official debut as an Olympic sport.

Changquan combines speed, kicks, jumps and acrobatics while taijiquan is akin to tai chi and involves controlled movements which flow together in a precise performance set to music.

National team uniforms were dispensed with to allow competitors to wear their own flowing robes, which were often brightly coloured and enhanced with detailed designs.

"Everybody has a different kind of flavour to their moves," the United States' Marshall Brayton said.

"I think that uniqueness in every person's routine is the essence of wushu."

As jumps, flips and flourishes with weaponry caught the eye in changquan, setting moves to music came with its own challenges in tajiquan.

"I was advised to sleep to the song (used in performance)," eventual champion Zhe Nin Ng of Singapore said after day two of competition.

"I had to understand it more and have it in my muscle memory. I keep playing it again and again until I fall asleep."

All you need to know about the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympics

While rowing has been an Olympic staple since 1900, a new twist has been added with the arrival of this discipline on Senegal's Atlantic coast.

The competition begins on dry land with an athlete running down the beach, boarding their boat and rowing out 250m to a marker buoy before turning sharply and racing back.

Once they return to shore, they then jump out of the boat and sprint back up the beach to touch a buzzer on the finish line. The fastest time wins.

"It's super fun. It's a lot more exciting than traditional rowing," 17-year-old USA's Isaac Moos told Olympics.com.

Beachfront spectators have the benefit of being able to witness a whole race and the unpredictability of sea conditions adds an extra element to competition.

"The waves are constantly changing and one small mistake can cost you," said Su Juntao, who won gold for China in the mixed double sculls.

"You have to push for more speed while keeping your mistakes to a minimum. That's what makes it so challenging and exciting."

And this is just the start for coastal rowing at the Olympics, because it is set to replace the lightweight double sculls category at LA 2028.

Baseball will also be included on the schedule in California in four years' time, but an urban, simplified version of the sport kicked off the action in Dakar last Friday.

Introduced to increase accessibility and taking inspiration from street games, the five-a-side version does not require equipment and featured mixed-gender teams on its Olympic debut.

With no pitcher, players for the 'batting' side using their hand to hit the rubber ball from a standing position on an 18m x 18m court featuring four bases.

There are no strikes, meaning each 'batter' gets just one chance to hit the ball legally as they attempt to score as many runs as possible before their team suffers three outs.

Played over five innings, it is faster-paced than its bigger brother and skills are rewarded over strength.

Cuba, the nation at the top of the all-time Olympic baseball medal table with three golds, fittingly opened the competition with a victory over Turkey.

"We have baseball running through our veins and in our hearts, and we will always, always, always put Cuba at the top," player Jean Carlos Machado Casado told Olympics.com.

While Olympics fans are used to seeing beach volleyball, two more traditional sports have been given a twist in Senegal.

Handball and wresting events have also been relocated to Saly's beach, known for its fine sand and turquoise waters.

Featured in continental and world championships, and promotional events organised by governing body United World Wrestling, beach wrestling fittingly makes its Youth Olympics debut in Senegal, where traditional forms of wrestling remain incredibly popular.

Two athletes contest bouts inside a circular area on sand, scoring points through throws, takedowns, or forcing the opponent out of bounds.

Matches, to be contested this weekend, are expected to be short and fast-paced.

Eight-a-side handball, which also featured at the Buenos Aires Youth Games in 2018, will be among the final events contested at Dakar 2026.

Skateboarding, first included in the senior Olympic schedule at Tokyo 2020, also made its Youth Games debut in Dakar.

articles.title: 15-year-old Tanvi Patri scripts history, becomes first Indian woman to win Youth Olympics badminton medal
articles.summary: At just 15, Odisha's Tanvi Patri becomes the first Indian woman to win a badminton medal at the Youth Olympic Games.
articles.body: At just 15, Odisha's Tanvi Patri becomes the first Indian woman to win a badminton medal at the Youth Olympic Games. Her remarkable silver-medal run in Dakar was a story of composure, courage and extraordinary fighting spirit, highlighted by a stunning comeback in the final against China's reigning World Junior Champion Zhang Yi Xin.India's Tanvi Patri scripted a historic chapter in Indian badminton after clinching the silver medal in the women's singles event at the 2026 Youth Olympic Games in Dakar, Senegal. The 15-year-old from Odisha became the first Indian woman to reach a badminton final and win a medal at the Youth Olympics, marking a significant milestone for the country's junior badminton circuit.However, the road to the podium was anything but straightforward. Tanvi's campaign was defined by her ability to rise to the occasion, particularly in the knockout stages, where she displayed remarkable composure against some of the tournament's strongest opponents.The young shuttler eventually settled for silver after an 82-minute battle against China's reigning World Junior Champion Zhang Yi Xin in the gold-medal match. Tanvi went down 15-21, 21-13, 24-26 in a thrilling three-game encounter, but her spirited fightback in the deciding game ensured that her performance would be remembered long after the final point.A fightback that nearly produced goldThe final against Zhang was a test of Tanvi's temperament and endurance. After losing the opening game 15-21, the Indian bounced back impressively to take the second game 21-13 and force a decider.The third game, however, appeared to be slipping away from her when she found herself trailing 10-19. With the gold medal seemingly within Zhang's grasp, Tanvi produced an extraordinary response, refusing to surrender despite the mounting pressure.She saved five consecutive match points to draw level at 24-24, turning what looked like a comfortable finish for the Chinese shuttler into a tense battle. Tanvi even earned three opportunities to seal the gold medal herself, but Zhang held her nerve in the closing exchanges to eventually prevail 26-24.Although the defeat denied her the gold, Tanvi's determination to fight until the very end stood out as one of the defining moments of the tournament.Tanvi Patri's road to the Youth Olympics finalThe 15-year-old, who trains at the Prakash Padukone Badminton Academy (PPBA), entered the competition as the third seed and enjoyed a strong start in the group stage.Quarterfinal: A historic semifinal entryTanvi faced Thailand's seventh-seeded Kakanik Kungkaew in the quarterfinals, with a place in the medal rounds at stake. The Indian youngster delivered a composed performance, winning 21-17, 21-13 in just 39 minutes. The straight-games victory not only secured her a semifinal berth but also made her the first Indian woman to reach the badminton semifinals at the Youth Olympic Games.Semifinal: Tanvi holds her nerve against Japan's second seedThe semifinal against Japan's second-seeded Yuzuno Watanabe proved to be a much tougher examination.Tanvi began confidently, taking the opening game 21-14 with an aggressive approach and precise shot-making. However, Watanabe responded strongly in the second game, capitalising on Tanvi's errors to level the contest with a 21-11 win.With a place in the final on the line, the Indian youngster needed to produce her best badminton in the deciding game. She managed to regain control of the rallies, improved her attacking approach and kept her composure in the closing stages.In a closely contested decider, Tanvi edged past Watanabe 21-19 to book her place in the gold-medal match.The victory was another landmark moment, making her the first Indian woman to reach a badminton final at the Youth Olympics.Joins elite company of Indian badminton medallistsTanvi's silver medal also adds to India's growing legacy in badminton at the Youth Olympic Games. She joins H.S. Prannoy, who won silver in 2010, and Lakshya Sen, who secured silver in 2018, as Indian badminton players to have reached the podium at the prestigious multi-sport event.More importantly, her achievement marks a first for Indian women's badminton at the tournament.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Goiânia poderá ter apenas uma corrida de rua por dia em 2027 | G1
articles.standfirst: De acordo com a Secretaria de Esporte e Lazer e a Federação Goiana de Atletismo, a recomendação da realização de apenas uma corrida por dia já existia, mas não era normatizada.
articles.summary: De acordo com a Secretaria de Esporte e Lazer e a Federação Goiana de Atletismo, a recomendação da realização de apenas uma corrida por dia já existia, mas não era normatizada.
articles.body:
Corrida celebra o Dia Internacional da Mulher em Goiânia — Foto: Wildes Barbosa/O Popular

A Prefeitura de Goiânia , por meio da Secretaria Municipal de Esporte e Lazer, publicou uma portaria sobre o Calendário Municipal de Corridas de Rua para o ano de 2027. Segundo o documento, durante o próximo ano será permitida a realização de apenas uma corrida de rua por dia. Além disso, a solicitação para os eventos deve ocorrer exclusivamente por meios eletrônicos (veja detalhes das regras abaixo) .

A portaria nº 42/2026 foi publicada no Diário Oficial do Município nesta terça-feira (3) e especifica as regras e critérios estabelecidos para a realização de corridas de rua em Goiânia no próximo ano.

🏁 De acordo com a secretaria e a Federação Goiana de Atletismo, a recomendação da realização de apenas uma corrida por dia já existia, mas não era normatizada.

Solicitação exclusivamente eletrônica: pedidos devem ser feitos entre 1º e 13 de novembro de 2026, por meio do Processo Eletrônico Digital (PED) no sistema E-RESOLVE;

Limite diário de eventos: fica estipulada a realização de apenas uma corrida por dia na cidade;

Ordem de envio: enviar o pedido no primeiro dia não garante prioridade na escolha da data;

Eventos tradicionais: eventos com realização de no mínimo 5 edições em 5 anos distintos têm prioridade na manutenção da data;

Datas remanescentes: a distribuição ocorre em rodadas sucessivas, com prioridade para quem tem menos datas;

Proibição de comercialização: fica proibida a comercialização, cessão ou transferência de datas reservadas.

De acordo com a portaria, a limitação de uma corrida por dia foi uma recomendação da Secretaria de Trânsito Municipal. O resultado preliminar do calendário será publicado até o dia 23 de novembro de 2026. Os solicitantes poderão apresentar recurso em até dois dias úteis após a divulgação.

Segundo o secretário de Esporte e Lazer, Luiz Alberto Sardinha Bites, a determinação que limita a quantidade de eventos diários era uma recomendação que visava a capacidade operacional da Secretaria de Trânsito, mas nunca havia sido normatizada.

"Existia, pela secretaria de trânsito, um acordo de realização dentro da capacidade deles. Porque o maior problema para eles é o efetivo para poder fazer, além dos outros eventos todos, duas corridas de rua", explicou.

De acordo com ele, o crescimento das corridas de rua motivou a formalização da regra para que os usuários das vias onde os percursos acontecem não sejam prejudicados. Ainda segundo o secretário, existe a possibilidade de acontecer duas corridas por dia, desde que a Secretaria Municipal de Engenharia de Trânsito avalie a situação.

O Circuito Junino em sua segunda edição, em Goiânia - Goiás — Foto: Fábio Lima/Opopular

Em entrevista ao g1 , Genivaldo José Caixeta, presidente da Federação Goiana de Atletismo, disse que essa recomendação é seguida pela federação "sem nenhum problema" e que quando houve a realização de mais de um evento por dia na cidade, foi com a autorização especial de órgãos competentes do município.

A proprietária da Bee Sports, empresa que organiza eventos esportivos em Goiânia, entende que a limitação a um evento por dia é prejudicial tanto ao mercado quanto às pessoas que praticam o esporte. Ao g1 , Ludmila Carneiro disse que acha a medida prejudicial.

"É um mercado gigante em expansão. Hoje, se nós falarmos em tirar pessoas do sedentarismo, eu acho que não tem nenhum esporte que faça isso mais do que a corrida. A gente tá falando de centenas e centenas de pessoas. Se restringir a uma corrida por dia, isso vai prejudicar até nisso", disse ela.

Segundo o presidente da federação, as provas autorizadas pela prefeitura continuam passando pelo crivo da federação, que vai analisar o regulamento da prova, as condições técnicas para a realização do evento, critérios de segurança e outras exigências para a emissão da autorização por parte da federação.

articles.title: At 93, the battles of Tokyo still live on in Dharam Singh Mann's memory
articles.summary: JALANDHAR: Dharam Singh Mann may have put away his hockey stick decades ago, but his passion for the game remains undiminished.
articles.body: JALANDHAR: Dharam Singh Mann may have put away his hockey stick decades ago, but his passion for the game remains undiminished. At 93, one of Punjab's oldest surviving links to Indian hockey's golden era, Mann played in the gold-medal-winning team at the 1964 Tokyo Olympics and the bronze-winning side at the 1968 Mexico Games. He vividly remembers the bruises, battles and bonds that shaped his journey.As Jalandhar, the heartland of Indian hockey, hosted the initial rounds of the Asian Champions Trophy, Mann served as a poignant reminder of a glorious legacy the sport must cherish and pass on to future generations.A retired Assistant Sub-Inspector (ASI) with Punjab Police, Mann began his journey on the village grounds, where his first hockey stick was his father's. "I used to take his stick and wait for my turn outside the village ground. The day I got my first chance, there was no looking back," he told TOI.Mann's international journey gathered momentum with the 1963 Lyon International Hockey Tournament in France, a key preparatory event ahead of the Tokyo Olympics. He also suffered a broken jaw after being struck by a rival's stick. He remembers the care he received from hockey legend Udham Singh, who brought him homemade desi ghee-bone broth and fed him for days as he recovered.Despite his age, memories of the 1964 Olympic final against Pakistan refuse to fade. When the old rivals targeted India's centre-forward Harbinder Singh, Mann and teammates Prithipal Singh and Gurbax Singh decided not to let the intimidation go unanswered. "We told him the game wasn't over. We would challenge them on the field like it's war," he recalled with a smile. India eventually prevailed, winning Olympic gold.During a visit to a primary school in Japan, Mann was struck by children who, instead of talking about what they wanted to become, asked what they could do for their country. He believes this sense of collective responsibility was central to Japan's sporting success and carried that lesson into hockey and the Punjab Police.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Fresh core group for LA 2028 as Indian men’s hockey team eye generational shift
articles.summary: MOHALI: The Indian men’s hockey team is preparing for a generational transition ahead of the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, with Hockey India chief selector
articles.body: MOHALI: The Indian men’s hockey team is preparing for a generational transition ahead of the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, with Hockey India chief selector RP Singh indicating that a fresh core group will soon be assembled and that four to six senior players, or potentially more, could make way as the national setup begins planning for the next Olympic cycle.Having completed a successful Asian Games campaign and secured Olympic qualification, India’s focus has now shifted from immediate results to long-term team building.“We have to build the team for 2028,” Singh said, stressing that the new core group would comprise a mix of established internationals and emerging talent.“It could be four players, it could be six, maybe fewer or even more players will be replaced. Nothing is fixed. But we have to look ahead and prepare the next generation.”Moreover, the core group will not be a closed group and will be reviewed at regular intervals.“We also want the core group to remain dynamic. Every three to six months, players must be reassessed. If someone is no longer operating at the required level, we should have the flexibility to make changes,” he added.Singh, however, emphasised that selection would be dictated by performance and fitness rather than reputation, age or seniority. “Seniority-based selection should not happen. It should be performance-based. Whoever is fit, performing and contributing to the team will remain in contention,” he said.The chief selector revealed that discussions about the future composition of the squad had already taken place within the management group, adding that difficult decisions are an unavoidable part of elite sport.“It hurts when players who have served the country for 10 or 12 years move out, but that is the reality of sport. One player leaves and another gets an opportunity,” he said.Opportunities will now be extended to more younger players through upcoming assignments, including the New Zealand tour, as India begins building towards the next Olympic cycle.Singh also confirmed that the Hockey India League is expected to return and could begin in Jan, describing the tournament as a crucial component of India's succession planning.The former India player also stressed the importance of exposing young Indian players to top European sides such as the Netherlands, Belgium, Germany and England, arguing that regular matches against elite opposition would accelerate their development and better prepare them for major tournaments.With the Los Angeles Olympics now firmly in sight, Indian hockey's transition has effectively begun, with performance, fitness and potential set to determine who forms the country's next core group.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Near miss inspires Martin to aim for Olympic medals
articles.summary: Abi Martin says her near-miss at the World Gymnastics Championships has inspired her to aim for the podium at the 2028 Olympic Games.
articles.body:
Abi Martin says a near miss at the World Gymnastics Championships has inspired her to aim for the podium at the 2028 Olympic Games.

Martin, 18, had the same score as France's bronze medallist Maiana Prat in the floor, but the French gymnast's better execution score saw the British competitor finish fourth.

It was the 2025 floor bronze medallist's second fourth place in a major event this year, having narrowly missed out in the vault at the European Championships.

"If anything it actually gives me fire in my belly because I think I struggled last year when I won the bronze, as much as it sounds crazy," she told BBC South West.

"I struggled knowing what to do next, whereas now, because I've got so close so many times, it's almost like next year I want to get it."

She continued: "Something that I've taken which I didn't actually realise is I'm the only gymnast that made the floor final in both World Championships in this cycle so far, so last year and this year.

"So I think I've taken from that that I am good enough to be in the mix and I know that I can be better.

"I think I made a slight mistake on the last tumble which showed that I can do it and I have been working hard, but I know that there's still more."

The Paignton-based gymnast won two silver medals and a bronze at this summer's Commonwealth Games.

She was also part of the Great Britain squad that won European team silver in 2024 and finished fourth at the last Olympic Games in Paris.

But despite that experience and her championship pedigree, Martin says she struggled with her self-belief at the start of 2026.

"I feel like I go through stages. At the beginning of this year I actually had a bit of a bad time with training," she said.

"I didn't really believe that I was good enough to do the stuff I was trying to do, which then affected how I was training and ultimately affected the results of the competitions.

"But luckily I had like the best team around me to pull me out of that hole and I've achieved a lot since then."

Her restored self-belief has helped Martin firmly set her sights on Los Angeles for the 2028 Olympics.

As one of the country's most experienced competitors she says her aim is to help Team GB continue its run of winning at least one Olympic gymnastics medal that stretches back to 2008.

"I would love to firstly make the team, but I think I have a lot bigger goals than just being on the Olympic team," she added.

"I'd love to stand on the podium, I'd love to win a medal with the team and individually - and I think it could be possible.

"I think next year my aims are to make the major championships again, the European Championships and the World Championships.

"The aim for the team, it's going to be a big year, is we need to get the Olympic qualification.

"For me personally I would love to aim for another major medal and a few more major finals."

articles.title: Bolt felicita a Cristiano por su carrera en la selección... ¡con una foto en MARCA!
articles.standfirst: El exvelocista, amigo del luso desde su etapa en el Manchester United, aseguró tras el anunció de su retirada de la selección que "nos hiciste fans a todos"
articles.summary: El exvelocista, amigo del luso desde su etapa en el Manchester United, aseguró tras el anunció de su retirada de la selección que "nos hiciste fans a todos"
articles.body: Usain Bolt, plusmarquista mundial de 100 y 200 metros, felicitó a Cristiano Ronaldo por su carrera en la selección portuguesa el día que anunció su adiós de la misma y lo hizo con una imagen de la visita que ambos deportistas realizaron a la redacción de MARCA en 2009. El jamaicano felicitó a Cristiano en redes sociales "por tu retirada del fútbol internacional. Nos hiciste fans a todos". Y acompañó el tuit con la fotografía de un pulso que dirimieron en el periódico. Aquel año, 2009, fue el del fichaje del futbolista luso por el Real Madrid, procedente del Manchester, mientras que Usain Bolt acababa de proclamarse campeón del mundo de 100 y 200, con récords mundiales incluidos que siguen vigentes, y de 4x100. Ambos deportistas se conocían de la etapa de Cristiano en el club inglés y así lo recordó el jamaicano en aquella entrevista en MARCA a finales de agosto. "La primera vez que oí hablar de él fue en un viaje a Manchester. Recuerdo que conocí a Ferguson, me invitó a un entrenamiento y allí le conocí. Me fijé en él por un golazo que marcó en la sesión", aseguró el atleta. También Cristiano se deshizo en elogios hacia Usain "Es el mejor velocista de la historia, soy un fan suyo", dijo. Entonces el jamaicano admitió que se había hecho del Real Madrid. "Es el mejor equipo del mundo", aseguró. Y ambos deportistas pidieron su particular deseo en la redacción de MARCA: "Queremos ser los mejores de la historia", aseguraron.

articles.title: Rober Alaiz anuncia su retirada: "Quizá no sea el final que imaginé. Pero es el que hoy necesito"
articles.standfirst: El atleta, de 36 años, se despide del atletismo de élite después de que las lesiones no le hayan permitido rendir al máximo
articles.summary: El atleta, de 36 años, se despide del atletismo de élite después de que las lesiones no le hayan permitido rendir al máximo
articles.body: Rober Alaiz anunció que se retira del atletismo de élite. Con un emotivo mensaje en redes, el fondista, de 36 años, aseguró que "se hizo tarde demasiado pronto. Después de muchos buenos años y de otros no tan buenos, ha llegado el momento de cerrar mi etapa como atleta profesional". Así, el leonés, que en los últimos años había estado inmerso en el maratón, explicó que "de un tiempo a esta parte siento que algo dentro de mí ha dejado de acompañarme cuando me pongo un dorsal en el pecho. Aquello que durante tantos años fue tan sencillo —sufrir y disfrutar al mismo tiempo— parece haberse convertido en algo inalcanzable, sobre todo cuando hace tiempo que no consigo ver ningún rayo de sol. Cada objetivo termina demasiado lejos de lo que esperaba, de lo que creo que podía dar y, sobre todo, de lo que algún día fui capaz de hacer". Alaiz, que no pudo cumplir uno de los sueños de su carrera, competir en unos Juegos, explicó que "durante mucho tiempo he vivido persiguiendo una versión de mí mismo que parecía estar siempre un poco más adelante. Después de tantas lesiones, volví con un sueño: llegar a unos Juegos Olímpicos. Un sueño que, durante mucho tiempo, dio sentido a muchos sacrificios. Creedme que he intentado encontrar respuestas de todas las maneras posibles, pero una vez más he errado". El leonés mostró otro deseo, que le permitirá seguir compitiendo a otro nivel: "Quiero volver a correr como cuando era un niño cuando no había aplausos ni halagos, sin el ego intrínseco del deportista. Quiero volver a hacerlo para ayudar a mi club, por mis amigos y por todas esas personas que han seguido a mi lado durante este camino. Quizá no sea el final que imaginé. Pero es el que hoy necesito. Gracias".

articles.title: Olympic champion Imane Khelif to make professional boxing debut in December
articles.summary: The Algerian has not fought since winning gold at Paris 2024, where she was embroiled in a gender row.
articles.body:
Olympic champion Imane Khelif has announced she will make her professional boxing debut next month in Paris, her first appearance in the ring since winning welterweight gold in the French capital in 2024.

Algeria’s Khelif, who found herself in the middle of a major gender row at the 2024 Olympics, holds a pro licence from France’s boxing federation and was forced to postpone her return to action in April after suffering a training injury.

The 27-year-old said during a news conference on Friday alongside her coach Kamel Abdesselam and promoter Yacin Berrabah that she will take on Clarida Sarabia in the super-welterweight class on December 15.

“It’s been over two years since I last boxed, and I’ve really missed being in the ring,” said Khelif.

“The last couple of years have been quite difficult. The time has come to turn professional, and I’m going to give it my all.”

Abdesselam is confident that Khelif could win a world title “within three to five fights” and compared his fighter with Muhammad Ali.

“We want to put Imane on top of the world,” said Abdesselam.

Frequently accused of being a transgender athlete, Khelif was born female but naturally carries the SRY gene, located on the Y chromosome, that indicates masculinity.

In February, she revealed in an interview with French sports daily L’Equipe that she had undergone hormonal treatment to lower her testosterone levels ahead of the Paris Olympics.

images.caption: Khelif celebrates winning a gold medal in the women’s 66kg boxing competition at the Paris 2024 Olympics [Andrew P Scott/USA TODAY Sports via Reuters]

articles.title: PV Sindhu, Harmanpreet Singh to chair, vice-chair, respectively, the IOA Athletes’ Commission
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Olympic medallists PV Sindhu and Harmanpreet Singh will helm the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) Athletes’ Commission, according to a
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Olympic medallists PV Sindhu and Harmanpreet Singh will helm the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) Athletes’ Commission, according to a notification issued by the Electoral Officer on Friday.Sindhu will become the chairperson of the Athletes’ Commission, while Harmanpreet has been declared unopposed for the post of vice-chairperson. Mirabai Chanu and Sajan Prakash will represent the commission in the IOA General Assembly, with one seat each reserved for a female and a male representative.The latest notification follows scrutiny of the four nominations received by 5 pm on November 5. It states that Sindhu was the only candidate to file a nomination for the chairperson’s post, while Harmanpreet was the sole nominee for vice-chairperson.Similarly, Chanu, a female candidate, and Prakash, a male candidate, were the only nominees for the two representatives’ positions in the IOA General Assembly.Under Rule 7 of the Athletes’ Commission Rules, 2026, the final list of contesting candidates, published in Form 6, has been deemed unopposed. The Electoral Officer has therefore stated that the election scheduled for November 7 will serve no purpose, as there is only one candidate for each post.The notification also states that the declaration of results under Form 9 will be published on November 7, in accordance with the earlier election notification dated November 3.The four appointments will give the Athletes’ Commission its representatives across two levels of the IOA structure.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: For Tanvi Patri’s father, Youth Olympic silver is just the beginning
articles.summary: KOLKATA: As Tanvi Patri produced one of the most remarkable fightbacks during the badminton girls’ singles final of Youth Olympic Games, her father
articles.body: KOLKATA: As Tanvi Patri produced one of the most remarkable fightbacks during the badminton girls’ singles final of Youth Olympic Games, her father Rabinarayan Patri was not in the stands witnessing it unfold.Instead, he was rushing through an airport, trying to catch a flight.What followed was an emotional roller-coaster. The 15-year-old Indian clawed her way back from 10-19 down in the deciding game against reigning world junior champion Zhang Yi Xin, saved six match points and even earned three of her own before eventually falling 15-21, 21-13, 24-26 in a marathon contest in Dakar on Thursday night.For many, it was a heartbreaking defeat. For her father, it was something else entirely.“Before the match, I told Tanvi that I would be happy even if she won a silver medal. I told her to enjoy the game, play for herself and play for the country,” Rabinarayan told TOI from Dubai on Friday.The close finish naturally left him wondering what might have been.“At 24-23 in the final game, one smash just missed the line. That was purely down to luck. Otherwise, she could have won it. But what makes me happy is that she finished the tournament healthy. That is the most important thing for me.”Tanvi came into the tournament after falling ill during the World Junior Championships following a long journey, and also had to contend with Dakar's heat, lack of air conditioning and mosquitoes.Despite those challenges, the result marked another milestone in the rapid rise of the Odisha shuttler who trains at the Centre for Badminton Excellence (CBE) in Bengaluru.Yet Rabinarayan insists neither he nor his daughter have allowed themselves to become consumed by junior results.“She called me after the match from the washroom and was crying. She said, ‘Papa, I lost.’”His response was immediate.“I told her to forget it because past is past. She had already achieved something wonderful. I reminded her that this is just the junior circuit. People may remember the result for a month or two, but that is not what defines a career.”For him, the destination remains much bigger than a Youth Olympic title.“The real target is an Olympic medal. Winning a junior title is good, but not winning it is not the end of the world. She won a silver medal and fought all the way. It was not as though she was outplayed. She gave a tremendous fight, and people saw her potential.”For now, though the focus will now shift to participating in a series of events after injuries disrupted much of her year. She is scheduled to compete in Indonesia, the Syed Modi International in Lucknow, the Guwahati Masters, the Odisha Masters and then the Senior National Championships.“It will be a challenging stretch. We may not perform well in every tournament, and that is okay,” he said. “The important thing is that she continues gaining experience against a variety of opponents on the senior circuit.”Strength and conditioning will also remain key areas of focus in the coming year.But for a father whose daughter came within a whisker of Youth Olympic gold, the outlook remains uncomplicated. “I want her to enjoy the game, compete without fear and develop the mindset needed at the highest level.”And if Dakar is any indication, the 15-year-old is doing exactly that.While the silver medal was the biggest achievement of her young career, Tanvi's favourite memories from the Games had little to do with the podium. “My most memorable moments were trading pins, making new friends and playing games in the 365 Athlete House,” she said.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: El japonés Honda no estará en los Juegos tras ser suspendido 21 meses por un accidente de tráfico
articles.standfirst: El nadador, subcampeón olímpico de 200 mariposa, ha recibido el castigo de la Federación de su país después de un accidente provocado por exceso de velocidad en 2025
articles.summary: El nadador, subcampeón olímpico de 200 mariposa, ha recibido el castigo de la Federación de su país después de un accidente provocado por exceso de velocidad en 2025
articles.body: Tomoru Honda, campeón mundial de 200 metros mariposa en 2024 y subcampeón olímpico de la prueba en 2020, no podrá competir en los próximos Juegos de Los Ángeles después de haber recibido una suspensión de 21 meses por parte de la Federación de su país. El nadador, que sufrió un accidente de tráfico en 2025 por exceso de velocidad (80 km/h) en el que invadió el carril contrario en un tramo en el que había que transitar a 30 km/h y chocó con otro conductor que resultó herido, ya recibió en septiembre una sentencia de prisión suspendida de un año, con tres años de libertad condicional. Esta sanción federativa, añadida a la multa que debió pagar (unos 8.500 euros), le impedirá buscar el podio en la próxima cita olímpica. El nadador no pudo competir en los Campeonatos Pan-Pacífico ni en los posteriores Juegos Asiáticos. En su comunicado, Federación Japonesa de Natación señaló que considera el incidente con gran seriedad y anunció planes para reforzar los programas de formación en materia de cumplimiento normativo y conducta de los deportistas.

articles.title: Olympics once gave out medals for poetry: First literature gold in 1912 went to the Games’ own founder, who had entered under two fake names
articles.summary: Discover the intriguing history of the Olympic arts competitions, including the art of poetry, and learn how Pierre de Coubertin won the first literature gold medal under a pseudonym at the 1912 Olympics.
articles.body: At the 1912 Stockholm Olympics, competitors could win gold without running, jumping or throwing anything. They could submit a poem, compose a piece of music, design a building or produce a sculpture, provided their work had something to do with sport. The arrangement was the fulfilment of an ambition held by Pierre de Coubertin, founder of the modern Olympic Games, who believed that the competition was incomplete without the arts. He was also sufficiently convinced of his own literary credentials to enter the first contest, although the judges had no idea who they were rewarding.The ancient ideal behind Coubertin’s Olympic visionCoubertin’s idea was not simply to make the Olympics more cultured, or to provide spectators with something to admire between athletic events. He was attempting to restore a relationship between physical achievement and artistic expression that he believed had been lost over centuries. The distinction mattered to him because he regarded the ancient Olympic tradition as something considerably more expansive than a gathering of athletes.At the Games in ancient Greece, competitors were not the only figures attracting attention. Poets also travelled to Olympia, where they recited their work before audiences and celebrated athletic victories through commissioned odes. The lyric poet Pindar became particularly associated with this tradition, writing elaborate victory poems for successful competitors, which were performed by choruses during public celebrations. The athlete’s achievement could thus become the subject of a literary work, with physical prowess and artistic accomplishment occupying the same cultural space.The idea had a philosophical lineage as well. Plato’s Republic described an education that combined gymnastics for the body with music for the soul, while the classical ideal of harmony offered Coubertin a model for the kind of individual he wanted the modern Olympics to recognise. He later described this balance as the reunion of two estranged partners, “muscle and mind”, whose separation had impoverished both.The historical circumstances of his youth helped shape that conviction. The first major excavations at Olympia began during the 1870s, uncovering extensive remains of the sanctuary that had hosted the ancient Games, along with thousands of artefacts. Coubertin was then a teenager in France, receiving a classical education at a Jesuit school after having encountered the ruins of ancient Rome during childhood family travels. The discoveries at Olympia gave a new immediacy to the ancient world he was studying.Richard Stanton, author of The Forgotten Olympic Art Competitions, told Smithsonian magazine in 2012 that Coubertin had been particularly impressed by the idea of an Olympian who possessed abilities beyond athletics, including knowledge of music and literature. Recreating the Games without some representation of the arts, Stanton explained, would have left the modern undertaking incomplete.A campaign to bring art back into the GamesThe first modern Olympics, held in Athens in 1896 after Coubertin helped establish the International Olympic Committee in 1894, contained no artistic competitions. The programme included events such as discus, swimming, fencing and pole vaulting, but the founder’s preferred marriage of intellectual and physical achievement remained largely theoretical. The addition of water polo and archery in 1900, followed by boxing and lacrosse in 1904, did little to address the imbalance.Coubertin continued to press his case, eventually turning the proposed artistic programme into a serious Olympic project. On August 5, 1904, he published an article titled “The Roman Olympiad” on the front page of the French newspaper Le Figaro, arguing that the modern Games should recover the character of their ancient predecessors. He wrote that, during Olympia’s period of splendour, “the arts and literature joined with sport to ensure the greatness of the Olympic Games”, and called for their return to the modern competition.The argument received a more formal hearing on May 23, 1906, when Coubertin convened the Consultative Conference on Art, Letters and Sport in the foyer of the Comédie-Française in Paris. Delegates considered how artistic disciplines might participate in the modern Olympics, including whether literary competitions could be organised and how sporting experiences might inspire writers. Coubertin’s opening address returned to his preferred metaphor, describing the separation of art and sport as a long estrangement between partners who had once enjoyed a fruitful relationship.The conference agreed that five artistic disciplines should be included at the 1908 Olympics: architecture, sculpture, painting, music and literature. Collectively, the competitions became known as the Pentathlon of the Muses, and the entries were required to be original works inspired by sport. The plan appeared settled until circumstances intervened in a manner that was particularly unfortunate for an undertaking already struggling to find its place.Mount Vesuvius erupted in the spring of 1906, killing about 200 people and causing considerable damage around Naples. Italy subsequently relinquished its plans to host the 1908 Olympics in Rome, with London taking over the event. The artistic competitions were postponed, leaving Coubertin to wait another four years before his project could finally appear on the Olympic programme.The founder enters under two assumed namesThe opportunity arrived at Stockholm in 1912, although the preparations were hardly encouraging. Interest among Sweden’s artistic community was limited, and the number of submissions threatened to make the entire undertaking look rather less impressive than Coubertin had imagined. Instead of abandoning the plan, he personally took charge of organising the competitions, which were divided into the five categories agreed upon six years earlier.The rules were straightforward enough. Works had to be original, connected thematically to sport and submitted within a specified period, after which a jury would select the winners. The first edition attracted only about three dozen competitors across all five disciplines, while the literature category received fewer than ten entries. One of those submissions came from two men who, as far as the judges knew, were Georges Hohrod and Martin Eschbach.Their entry, Ode to Sport, was awarded the sole gold medal in literature. Its authors were, in fact, Coubertin writing under pseudonyms believed to have been inspired by towns near his wife’s birthplace. The founder of the modern Olympics had not merely introduced an artistic competition; he had entered it himself and won its highest prize without disclosing his identity to the jury.The poem was a prose composition arranged in eight sections, each devoted to a different virtue associated with sport. Its opening address described sport as a “delight of the Gods” and a “distillation of life”, before moving through themes including honour, joy, progress and the physical pleasures of competition. The writing was expansive and unabashedly celebratory, reflecting the idealistic language of a man who saw athletics as a source of moral and cultural renewal.Modern readers may find its declarations excessive, but the Stockholm jury was considerably more enthusiastic. Its report described the poem as “far and away the winner in the literature competition”, praising its understanding of the inspiration the organisers wanted the category to reward. Coubertin eventually revealed that he had written the work, although the precise moment of disclosure did little to diminish the peculiar distinction attached to his victory.The competitions grow, but never quite find their audienceThe Stockholm numbers were modest, but participation increased during the following editions. By 1928, the arts competitions had attracted more than 1,000 entries, and the original five categories had developed into separate subcategories. Literature, for example, was divided into epic and lyric works, giving poets more defined opportunities to compete for medals.The expansion did not necessarily bring the prestige Coubertin had hoped to secure. The requirement that works be inspired by sport discouraged many established writers, leaving the competitions without the literary names that might have helped them attract wider attention. William Butler Yeats did not enter, although his brother Jack Butler Yeats won a silver medal in painting at the 1924 Paris Olympics. Robert Graves, one of Britain's prominent poets, entered the literature competition that year and later dismissed the experience in a letter as a “bad joke”.Some of the winning works have since acquired an unlikely afterlife through the efforts of historians trying to recover what the Olympic record books preserve only imperfectly. Among them was Sword Songs, the 37-page poem by Dorothy Margaret Stuart that won a silver medal in 1924. Tony Perrottet, author of The Naked Olympics, eventually located a copy at the New York Public Library, describing its dated language and occasional resemblance to a Monty Python sketch. Its sections moved through medieval Scotland, ancient Rome, Renaissance France and eighteenth-century Dunkirk, with one passage describing two warriors attempting to find openings in each other's armour.Other medal-winning works have proved harder to locate. Perrottet noted that poems such as Rudolf Binding's A Rider’s Instructions to His Lover, which won silver in Amsterdam in 1928, and Charles Gonnet's Before the Gods of Olympia, which received bronze in Paris in 1924, had seemingly disappeared. He suggested that the questionable literary quality of some entries might help explain why so many had not been preserved.The 1936 Berlin Olympics introduced another complication, as the artistic programme became entangled with the propaganda ambitions of Adolf Hitler and his regime. Joseph Goebbels, Hitler's propaganda minister, helped oversee that year's competitions, which awarded nine gold medals, five of them to German entrants. Germany won the lyric literature category, while Finland took the gold for epic literature. The only American medallist was Charles Downing Lay, who received silver for a town-planning design in the architecture competition.London 1948 and the end of the Olympic arts programmeBy the time the Olympics reached London in 1948, the artistic competitions had awarded approximately 150 medals across their various disciplines. Their history also included a distinction that is less frequently mentioned: Ernst van Heerden, a gay South African poet, won silver for lyric poetry that year, four decades before American equestrian Robert Dover became widely recognised as the first openly gay athlete to compete in the modern Olympics.The London edition proved to be the last. The central difficulty concerned the Olympic commitment to amateurism, which required competitors to remain unpaid in their sporting pursuits. Applying that principle to artists was complicated, since many writers, architects, musicians and painters earned their living through precisely the professional work they were being invited to submit. The distinction between amateur and professional artistic participation became increasingly difficult to maintain, while the quality and quantity of entries offered officials little reason to defend the programme.Avery Brundage, who became IOC president in 1952, was among the strongest opponents of the competitions. Stanton suggested that his position might have been influenced by personal disappointment, since Brundage had entered the literature category twice and received no more than an honourable mention. The artistic medals were eventually removed from official Olympic records, and occasional proposals to revive the competitions have failed to gain sufficient support.Coubertin did not live to see their disappearance. He died in 1937, but had already reflected on the resistance to his project in his Olympic memoirs, published in 1931. He identified the principal obstacle as “fear of the classical”, arguing that modern writers struggled to understand physical exertion, painters favoured approaches poorly suited to sporting scenes, and audiences had lost their appetite for open-air musical performances.His complaint about music was characteristically severe: “The public,” he wrote, “had completely lost all taste for open-air cantatas.”The artistic competitions did not transform the modern Olympics into the union of physical and intellectual achievement that Coubertin had imagined. They did, however, leave behind an unusual record of the period when Olympic champions could be poets, painters and composers, and when the founder himself could quietly collect a gold medal for a poem written under two assumed names.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates.
